questions.q: What distinguishes Continuous Deployment from Continuous Delivery?
options: Deployment releases every passing change to production automatically; delivery keeps every change releasable but a human decides when
questions.explain: Delivery has a manual gate; deployment doesn't.

questions.q: What does Continuous Integration require at minimum?
options: Frequent merges to a shared mainline, with every change automatically built and tested
questions.explain: Small frequent merges keep integration pain low.

questions.q: Why does the course say the pipeline ideas were demonstrated with minici rather than GitHub Actions?
options: No Actions runner or Jenkins server was available when it was written, so the ideas were run locally and the platform syntax comes from documentation
questions.explain: The course states honestly what was and wasn't run.

questions.q: Before CI/CD, what was the typical integration failure?
options: Weeks of separate branches merged the night before a release, producing a large, risky merge
questions.explain: CI shrinks the batch size.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions vocabulary, what is the `needs:` keyword for?
options: Declaring that a job depends on other jobs finishing first
questions.explain: It expresses ordering between jobs.

questions.q: Which is a job and which is a step?
options: A job is a unit of work on one runner with its own clean workspace; a step is one command or action inside it
questions.explain: Jobs run in parallel unless they declare needs.

questions.q: What is a trigger?
options: The event that starts a pipeline run, such as push, pull_request, schedule or manual dispatch
questions.explain: A pipeline should start for a reason you can name.

questions.q: In Jenkins Declarative pipelines, what plays the role GitHub's `runs-on:` plays?
options: agent { ... }, which selects the machine or container
questions.explain: Both name where work executes.

questions.q: What does `concurrency` with `cancel-in-progress: true` do in the sample workflow?
options: Cancels an older in-flight run of the same group when a newer one starts
questions.explain: The group is keyed by workflow and ref.

questions.q: Why does the sample set `permissions: contents: read`?
options: Least privilege: the token gets only read access unless a job asks for more
questions.explain: The default token may be read-write.

questions.q: What does a matrix of two Python versions with `fail-fast: false` do?
options: Runs both versions even if one fails, so you see every result
questions.explain: fail-fast: true cancels remaining cells.

questions.q: Why set `timeout-minutes` on a job?
options: A hung job would otherwise run until the platform limit, wasting hours
questions.explain: Linter rule W004 flags its absence.

questions.q: What's the Jenkins controller's job, and what should NOT run on it?
options: It hosts the UI, job definitions, credentials and queue; keep builds off it and run them on agents
questions.explain: Agents execute the work.

questions.q: How do jobs choose an agent?
questions.explain: Labels describe capabilities.

questions.q: What is the main operational burden of Jenkins plugins?
options: Each plugin is code with controller privileges, with its own update and vulnerability cadence
questions.explain: Plugin sprawl is a scaling risk.

questions.q: What does `parallel {}` inside a Declarative pipeline do?
options: Runs the contained stages at the same time
questions.explain: Sequential stages run in order.

questions.q: Two jobs: a 3-second integration suite that fails and a 0.1-second unit suite that fails. How does ordering affect feedback?
options: Running unit first reports the failure in 0.1 s versus 3.1 s: same checks, 30x faster feedback
questions.explain: Order gates by cost and likelihood of failing.

questions.q: What shape does the test pyramid recommend?
options: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests
questions.explain: The reverse (an ice-cream cone) is slow and flaky.

questions.q: Where should static checks like lint and type checks go?
options: First: they take seconds and catch cheap mistakes
questions.explain: Surface problems early and cheaply.

questions.q: What's a gate?
options: A check that must pass before a change moves on
questions.explain: Most pipeline value comes from the gates and their order.

questions.q: Which practice makes a build more reproducible?
options: Pin dependencies with a lockfile, the toolchain version and base images by digest
questions.explain: Otherwise the build is a function of the internet.

questions.q: What should a cache key be derived from?
options: The hash of the inputs, such as the lockfile, rather than the date
questions.explain: Same inputs, same key; changed lockfile, new key.

questions.q: Why is `image:latest` a reproducibility problem?
options: It's mutable: the same tag can point to a different image tomorrow
questions.explain: Use image@sha256 digests.

questions.q: What does a bit-for-bit reproducible build guarantee?
options: Two machines building the same inputs produce identical bytes, useful for supply-chain verification
questions.explain: It's a stronger goal than ordinary repeatability.

questions.q: What is the rule about promoting a build to production?
options: Build once and promote the same artifact (same digest) through staging to production
questions.explain: Rebuilding deploys something you never tested.

questions.q: Under Semantic Versioning, which change bumps MAJOR?
options: An incompatible change to the public API
questions.explain: MINOR is features, PATCH is fixes.

questions.q: Why mirror public dependencies in a private registry?
options: A public outage or package removal won't break your builds
questions.explain: The left-pad incident is the example.

questions.q: Why address a container image by digest as well as tag?
options: Tags can be moved; a digest identifies exact content
questions.explain: Immutability is the point of an artifact.

questions.q: A secret is committed then deleted in the next commit. Is it safe?
options: No: Git history keeps it, so revoke and rotate it
questions.explain: Treat it as compromised.

questions.q: Why are secrets passed on command lines risky?
options: They're visible to other processes (ps) and often logged
questions.explain: Prefer environment variables injected into only the needed step.

questions.q: Which pull-request scenario exposes secrets to untrusted code?
options: Workflows triggered by forks that can read secrets
Pull requests from the same repo with read-only tokens
questions.explain: Untrusted code must not receive secrets.

questions.q: What does 'scope narrowly, inject late' mean?
options: Give each environment/job only the secrets it needs, exposed only to the step that uses them
questions.explain: A single all-powerful token makes any leak catastrophic.

questions.q: Two branches each pass tests alone but fail when combined. What does this show?
options: PR checks must run on what will actually merge (the merged result), not the branch alone
questions.explain: A rename plus a new caller of the old name broke after the merge.

questions.q: Which branching strategy integrates continuously with very short-lived branches?
options: Trunk-based development, usually with feature flags
questions.explain: Longer-lived branches mean riskier merges.

questions.q: When is GitFlow a reasonable fit?
options: Software shipped in discrete versions with long support windows
questions.explain: It integrates per release.

questions.q: What should a PR pipeline answer within minutes?
options: Does it build, do tests/lint/type checks pass, are there security findings, who needs to review
questions.explain: Fast feedback before merge.

questions.q: In minici, what happens to a job whose dependency failed?
options: It's skipped unless it has `if: always()`
questions.explain: Same idea as GitHub's default behaviour.

questions.q: Why does minici refuse unsupported `${{ }}` expressions?
options: Silently ignoring them would make a pipeline appear to work while skipping logic
questions.explain: Fail loudly.

questions.q: Why run step scripts with `set -eo pipefail`?
options: So a failing command in a pipeline fails the step instead of being hidden
questions.explain: A step otherwise reports only the last command's status.

questions.q: When does the runner save a cache?
questions.explain: A failed build could save a poisoned cache.

questions.q: A 3x3 os/python matrix with one exclude and one include that matches no cell. How many jobs?
questions.explain: The unmatched include adds a new job.

questions.q: How does `exclude` match?
options: A combination is removed when it matches all the keys given; a partial pattern removes every combination containing those values
questions.explain: Include matches existing cells or adds a new one.

questions.q: When does `include` add a new job instead of extending an existing one?
options: When it matches no existing combination
questions.explain: This trips people up.

questions.q: Why is a matrix a trade-off?
options: It multiplies coverage but also compute minutes and queue time
questions.explain: Billed minutes sum every cell.

questions.q: The lockfile changes when a dependency is bumped. What happens to a lockfile-hash cache key?
options: It changes, so the cache rebuilds, and reverting restores the original key's entry
questions.explain: The key is deterministic over the inputs.

questions.q: Why hash a lockfile rather than a loose requirements list?
options: `flask>=3` resolves to different packages over time while its file hash stays the same
questions.explain: The key must capture what determined the contents.

questions.q: What are restore keys for?
options: Partial hits: restore the closest older cache when the exact key misses
questions.explain: Most packages didn't change.

questions.q: What is cache poisoning?
options: Bad content saved into a shared cache that later builds then trust
questions.explain: Scope caches and avoid saving from untrusted PRs.

questions.q: When should you choose a reusable workflow over a composite action?
options: For a few steps in one job
When the shared unit needs its own runner, permissions or matrix (it delegates a whole job)
questions.explain: Composite actions share steps inside a job.

questions.q: How do reusable workflows receive secrets, and which is preferred?
options: Passed explicitly or via `secrets: inherit`; explicit is preferred
questions.explain: Inputs are plain values, not secret.

questions.q: Why was the top-level `on` key read as the boolean True in PyYAML?
questions.explain: Tools parsing workflows must account for it.

questions.q: What is the gain of reusable pipelines across 15 repos?
options: One place to fix a security patch instead of fifteen copies
questions.explain: Reuse is a maintenance and security lever.

questions.q: A database service container is started but tests fail on the first query. Why?
options: Started is not ready: the process launched but isn't accepting queries; add a health check
questions.explain: The sample uses --health-cmd pg_isready.

questions.q: How do steps inside a `container:` job reach a service named db?
options: Via the host name db (the service name) on its port
questions.explain: Service name is the DNS name.

questions.q: What's the risk of `container: python:3.12-slim`?
options: The tag is mutable and may change under you; pin by digest for reproducibility
questions.explain: Mutable tags break reproducibility.

questions.q: What does this lesson say honestly about what was run?
options: No container was built or run; the syntax comes from documentation
questions.explain: No container runtime was available.

questions.q: A suite has 100 tests, each flaking with probability 0.1%. How often is it green on correct code?
questions.explain: Flakes compound: P(green) = (1-p)^n.

questions.q: A 500-test suite with a 1% per-test flake rate is green how often?
What is a flaky test?
options: One that passes and fails on the same code
questions.explain: A few hundred make the pipeline random.

questions.q: Why is rerunning until green a bad habit?
options: It hides flakes and teaches people to ignore red builds; fix or quarantine them with a flake budget
questions.explain: Trust in the pipeline erodes.

questions.q: A module has 100% line and branch coverage and a pricing bug passes the weak test suite. What does this show?
options: Coverage shows what code ran, not that behaviour was checked; assertions matter
questions.explain: A strong suite with the same coverage caught the bug.

questions.q: What does mutation testing check?
options: Whether tests fail when small changes (like > to >=) are made to the code
questions.explain: It gives evidence tests check behaviour.

questions.q: What is a quality gate?
options: A check whose failure blocks a merge or deployment
questions.explain: Examples: tests, coverage not dropping, lint, vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Which signal can coverage legitimately give?
options: Finding code that no test touches
questions.explain: It can't find missing assertions.

questions.q: Why attach secrets to an environment rather than the repository?
options: Repository secrets are visible to every job; environment secrets are only released to jobs that pass the environment's protection rules
questions.explain: Protection rules gate access.

questions.q: What do required reviewers do on an environment?
options: Pause the deploy job until an approver signs off
questions.explain: A waiting job doesn't consume a runner.

questions.q: What do branch restrictions on an environment do?
options: Allow only workflows from specific branches (e.g. main) to deploy there
questions.explain: They stop feature branches from deploying to production.

questions.q: What happens to a run waiting for approval for too long?
options: It's eventually cancelled (documented limit around 30 days)
questions.explain: Stale approvals silently expire.

questions.q: What's the main risk of a persistent self-hosted runner workspace?
options: Stale files from earlier builds can make a build pass or fail depending on leftovers
questions.explain: The lesson demonstrates this with minici.

questions.q: When is a self-hosted runner justified?
options: Needs hosted runners can't meet: GPUs, ARM, private network access, special hardware
questions.explain: You own patching and isolation.

questions.q: Which runs jobs in a fresh VM discarded afterwards?
questions.explain: Isolation is a hosted-runner strength.

questions.q: Why is running untrusted PR code on a persistent self-hosted runner dangerous?
options: It can persist malware or steal credentials between jobs
questions.explain: Use ephemeral runners for untrusted code.

questions.q: 30 services at 12 minutes each, run on every push: what's the cost?
options: About 6 hours of runner time per push
questions.explain: Hence path filters and affected-only builds.

questions.q: What does `paths:` do in a workflow trigger?
options: Runs the workflow only when changed files match the patterns
questions.explain: paths-ignore is the inverse.

questions.q: Why must path filters include shared libraries a service depends on?
options: A change in libs/common can break the service even if its own files didn't change
questions.explain: Missing dependencies lead to false greens.

questions.q: What does the course's pathfilter map?
options: Changed files to the projects they affect, tested with a real temporary Git repo
questions.explain: Nine tests pass.

questions.q: What does rule W003 flag?
options: `uses:` not pinned to a 40-hex commit SHA
questions.explain: Tags can be moved; a SHA cannot.

questions.q: Why is `pull_request_target` checking out the PR head dangerous (W002)?
options: Untrusted code runs with a privileged token and secrets
questions.explain: A classic supply-chain attack path.

questions.q: What is script injection (W005)?
options: Untrusted `${{ github.event... }}` text interpolated into a run: script, letting an attacker execute commands
questions.explain: Pass values via env instead.

questions.q: Why does a deploy job need `concurrency:` (W006)?
options: Two runs could deploy at once and the older one may finish last, leaving an old version live
questions.explain: Serialise deploys.

questions.q: Which strategy has downtime between stopping the old version and starting the new?
questions.explain: It's simple and fine for maintenance windows.

questions.q: What is the main risk of a rolling deployment?
options: Old and new versions serve traffic at the same time, so they must be compatible
questions.explain: Rolling replaces instances a few at a time.

questions.q: What does blue-green give you?
options: An instant switch of traffic, and an instant switch back while the old environment is kept alive
questions.explain: Cost: a whole second environment, and shared databases still need compatible changes.

questions.q: What does a canary release need to be safe?
options: Good metrics and enough traffic to detect a problem on the small share
questions.explain: Send traffic back to 0% to roll back.

questions.q: What do feature flags decouple?
options: Deploy (code on servers) from release (behaviour exposed to users)
questions.explain: A flag off means a deploy isn't a launch.

questions.q: Why is a percentage rollout based on a hash of flag and user id?
options: A user gets a consistent answer, and widening from 10% to 20% keeps the earlier 10% enabled (a subset)
questions.explain: The sample showed a 10% set is a subset of the 20% set.

questions.q: Why are flags the usual fastest rollback for a bad release?
options: Reverting a value takes seconds, no redeploy
questions.explain: Remove stale flags afterwards.

questions.q: What problem do long-lived flags cause?
options: Accumulated untested combinations and dead code paths
questions.explain: Clean up flags once rollout completes.

questions.q: Why does a direct `RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name` break a rolling deploy?
options: Old code still running (or after a rollback) queries `name` and fails immediately
questions.explain: Verified in SQLite in the lesson.

questions.q: What is the expand/migrate/contract pattern?
options: Add the new column compatibly, migrate data and code, then remove the old column in a later release
questions.explain: Each step is compatible with its neighbours.

questions.q: Why can't you just roll back a destructive schema change?
options: The data or column is gone, and old code breaks
questions.explain: Only additive changes are easy to roll back.

questions.q: What should the new column be at the expand step?
options: Nullable, with no constraint the old code would violate
questions.explain: Old code ignores it.

questions.q: Which change can a rollback restore?
options: Stateless application code and configuration/flag values
questions.explain: Redeploy the previous artifact or revert the value.

questions.q: Which of these can a rollback NOT undo?
options: External effects such as emails, payments and API calls
questions.explain: Plan forward fixes for such effects.

questions.q: In GitOps, what is a rollback?
options: A revert in Git that the reconciler applies
questions.explain: The simulator models this.

questions.q: Why is 'we can always roll back' risky?
options: It's only true for some changes; data and external effects may be irreversible
questions.explain: The most expensive sentence in delivery.

questions.q: What should run on every pull request in an infrastructure repo?
options: A plan, shown to reviewers, since one variable change can have large effects the HCL diff doesn't show
questions.explain: Plan on PRs, apply on merge.

questions.q: Why apply a saved plan (plan -out)?
options: It guarantees the applied change is exactly what was reviewed
questions.explain: A fresh plan on main may differ.

questions.q: How should credentials differ between plan and apply jobs?
options: Plan job read-only; apply job has write access only on the protected branch and environment
questions.explain: Separate credentials limit blast radius.

questions.q: Why serialise applies per state?
options: Concurrent applies could corrupt state; use locking and a concurrency group
questions.explain: One at a time per state.

questions.q: What is the GitOps reconciler's job?
options: Continuously compare desired state in Git with actual state and apply the difference
questions.explain: Create what's missing, update what differs, optionally prune extras.

questions.q: Someone sets web replicas to 10 by hand and adds a `debug` object. What does the simulator report?
options: Drift: web changed, debug extra; reconcile updates web and (with prune) deletes debug
questions.explain: Git remains the source of truth.

questions.q: What is the difference between push and GitOps deployment?
options: Push: CI applies to the target; GitOps: a reconciler pulls and applies from Git
questions.explain: Cluster credentials stay inside the cluster in the pull model.

questions.q: What does `prune` do?
options: Deletes objects that exist but aren't in Git
questions.explain: Without it extras survive.

questions.q: Under Conventional Commits, which commit bumps MAJOR?
options: `feat!: drop python 3.8` (or a BREAKING CHANGE footer)
questions.explain: ! marks a breaking change.

questions.q: Which bumps MINOR?
questions.explain: A new backward-compatible feature.

questions.q: Why use machine-readable commit messages?
options: A tool can compute the next version and write the changelog
questions.explain: semrel does this.

questions.q: What does a changelog serve?
options: Telling consumers what changed between releases so they can judge upgrade risk
questions.explain: Continuous delivery still needs release communication.

questions.q: What is dependency confusion?
options: A public package with the same name as your private one wins resolution
questions.explain: Use scoped registries.

questions.q: How do you defend against a moved tag on a third-party action?
options: Pin to a full commit SHA
questions.explain: A SHA can't be moved.

questions.q: What did the checksum demo show?
options: Tampering with an archive changes its SHA-256, so verification fails
questions.explain: Verify downloads.

questions.q: What is an SBOM for?
options: Listing a build's components so vulnerable dependencies can be found
questions.explain: It helps with transitive dependencies.

questions.q: Which are the four DORA measures?
options: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore
questions.explain: Two measure speed and two stability.

questions.q: On the fixture, lead times are 2, 4, 6 and 1 hours and two of four deploys failed. What are the average lead time and change failure rate?
A team deploys ten times a day with a 40% failure rate. Are they elite?
options: No: speed without stability isn't elite
Yes if lead time is short
questions.explain: Both pairs matter.

questions.q: Why not rank people by DORA metrics?
options: They measure the delivery system, and using them as targets invites gaming
questions.explain: Use them to find bottlenecks.

questions.q: Why is the canary test one-sided?
options: Only a worse canary matters; a better one isn't a reason to stop
questions.explain: A test asserts z < 0 doesn't roll back.

questions.q: Why require a minimum canary sample?
options: At 1% of 20,000 requests only 200 canary requests exist and a burst of errors can look dramatic
questions.explain: min_canary=400.

questions.q: What does the simulator do after the last step succeeds?
questions.explain: Otherwise it rolls back when z exceeds the limit.

questions.q: Why accumulate counts across steps?
options: More samples sharpen detection of a small increase in error rate
questions.explain: Each step adds evidence.

questions.q: What should you do first when threat-modelling a pipeline?
options: List what you're protecting (deploy credentials, source access, signing keys, secrets, artifacts, runners)
questions.explain: Then ask what an attacker could do with each.

questions.q: Why are signing keys a high-value asset?
options: An attacker can make malicious artifacts look genuine
questions.explain: Protect them in a vault or hardware-backed service.

questions.q: Why is a build cache a target?
options: Poisoning it can ship tampered code without touching the source
questions.explain: Scope and key caches carefully.

questions.q: Which earlier control does this lesson reuse?
options: The workflow linter that flags unpinned actions, missing permissions and script injection
questions.explain: Defence in depth.

questions.q: lint 1, build 4, unit 6 (3 cells, needs build), e2e 12 (needs build), deploy 2 (needs unit and e2e). What are the critical path and billed minutes?
options: 18 minutes (build 4 → e2e 12 → deploy 2) and 37 billed minutes
questions.explain: Wall-clock follows the longest dependency chain; billed time sums every job including each matrix cell.

questions.q: What's the difference between wall-clock time and compute time?
options: Wall-clock is what a developer waits; compute is total billed machine-minutes
questions.explain: Parallelism trades one for the other.

questions.q: Does splitting a 12-minute job across 3 runners reduce total compute?
options: No: it cuts wall-clock but total compute doesn't drop (and startup overhead adds)
questions.explain: Cost and speed are different dials.

questions.q: What is the best way to shorten a pipeline's latency?
options: Shorten the critical path: split or speed up the longest chain
Add jobs off the critical path
questions.explain: Work off the critical path doesn't change latency.

questions.q: Why shouldn't heavy logic live in a Jenkinsfile?
options: Pipeline scripts run in the controller's JVM, so heavy loops load the controller
questions.explain: Push work to agents and tools.

questions.q: What stops unbounded build history filling the controller disk?
options: Build discarders (keep N builds or N days)
questions.explain: Set sensible defaults.

questions.q: Why is configuration drift a problem for UI-configured Jenkins?
options: Changes aren't versioned or reproducible, so a rebuilt controller loses them; use configuration as code
questions.explain: JCasC is the remedy.

questions.q: What is plugin sprawl?
options: Hundreds of plugins from many maintainers, each running with controller privileges and its own update cadence
questions.explain: Reduce and review plugins.

questions.q: A job needs 8 hours. Where can it run?
options: Self-hosted runners (hosted jobs are capped at 6 hours), or split the work
questions.explain: Hosted ≤ 6 h; self-hosted ≤ 5 days.

questions.q: A matrix needs 400 cells. What's the constraint?
options: A matrix is limited to 256 jobs; split into several workflows or chunks
questions.explain: Design around documented limits.

questions.q: Why not build a 'retry until green' habit given re-run limits?
options: Re-runs are capped (documented 50 attempts) and hide flakes
questions.explain: Fix flakes instead.

questions.q: How do large caches interact with the 10 GB per repository limit?
options: They evict each other (LRU), so share keys and cache downloads
questions.explain: Design caches deliberately.

questions.q: Which evidence shows a change was reviewed by someone other than the author?
options: Pull-request approvals with identities and timestamps, enforced by branch protection
questions.explain: Evidence should be produced by the pipeline.

questions.q: What does separation of duties mean here?
options: The same person shouldn't be able to write, approve and deploy a risky change
questions.explain: Access reviews verify it.

questions.q: What does a hash-chained audit log give?
options: Tamper evidence: altering any earlier entry breaks the chain
questions.explain: It's a teaching model, not a certified product.

questions.q: What must be recorded about a deployment?
options: Version, artifact digest, commit SHA and build ID
questions.explain: Traceability answers 'what exactly was deployed?'.

questions.q: A pipeline contract test breaks a unit test and expects what?
options: The test job fails and packaging/deploy jobs are skipped
questions.explain: A false green is the worst failure.

questions.q: Why test the gates themselves?
options: A scan that quietly stops running looks green; verify it fails on known-bad input
questions.explain: A gate that never fails may not be running.

questions.q: What's a false red?
questions.explain: Both false green and false red erode trust.

questions.q: What does a workflow linter check that tests don't?
options: Config validity: YAML syntax, expression errors, references to jobs and secrets that don't exist
questions.explain: It's a different layer.

questions.q: A secret leaked in a repository. What's the first priority?
options: Revoke and rotate it, then investigate
questions.explain: Assume it's compromised.

questions.q: Main is red and nobody can merge. What's the first priority?
options: Restore green quickly by reverting or fixing forward
questions.explain: Broken main blocks everyone.

questions.q: A runaway matrix is burning budget. What do you do first?
options: Cancel the runs, cap spend, then fix the trigger
questions.explain: Stop the bleeding.

questions.q: Why know an emergency deploy path?
options: If the pipeline is down, you still need a controlled way to ship a fix
questions.explain: Pipeline outages stop all shipping.

questions.q: What's the first phase of a CI migration?
options: Decide why (valid reasons), then inventory everything
questions.explain: You can't migrate what you haven't found.

questions.q: What does wf2minici do for unsupported features?
options: Lists everything it can't translate rather than silently dropping it
questions.explain: Honest conversion.

questions.q: What should an inventory include for each pipeline?
options: Triggers, steps/tools, credentials, runner needs and downstream consumers
questions.explain: Downstream consumers rely on statuses and artifacts.

questions.q: What's a safe cutover technique?
options: Run old and new in parallel and compare results before switching required checks
questions.explain: Parallel runs find gaps.

questions.q: What is a golden path?
options: A supported, easy default route that bundles the secure, tested, observable way of shipping
questions.explain: Make the right way the easy way.

questions.q: What belongs on a Python service's golden path?
options: Layout, CI workflow with pinned tools, deploy pipeline with approvals, security baseline, observability, docs
questions.explain: Teams otherwise remake these decisions.

questions.q: How is a golden path verified?
options: By tests that check the generated workflow meets policy (pinned actions, permissions, timeouts)
questions.explain: goldenpath.py has eight tests.

questions.q: Why not force teams onto the path?
options: It should win by being easier; forcing breeds workarounds
questions.explain: Paved road, not a fence.

questions.q: When is a release `ready` in the capstone?
options: Only when the list of reasons is empty
questions.explain: Four independent checks collect reasons.

questions.q: Which four checks does readiness combine?
options: Workflow lint, infrastructure plan guard, DORA delivery health and a canary simulation
questions.explain: Each adds reasons.

questions.q: What happens if the canary simulator decides to roll back?
options: A reason is added and the release is not ready
questions.explain: Metrics include canary decision.

questions.q: What are the capstone's inputs?
options: Synthetic data: a generated workflow, a plan and hand-made deployments, not real team data
questions.explain: The lesson states it plainly.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes continuous delivery from continuous deployment?
options: Deployment is only for mobile apps
Delivery keeps every passing change releasable with a human release decision; deployment releases every passing change automatically
questions.explain: The difference is the manual gate.

questions.q: Same two failing checks: unit (0.1 s) and integration (3 s). Which order gives the fastest feedback?
options: Unit first, then integration: you learn about the failure in 0.1 s instead of 3.1 s
questions.explain: Order gates by cost and likelihood of failing.

questions.q: A team deploys with `image: python:3.12-slim` and sees a surprise change. Why?
options: Mutable tags can move to a different image; pin by digest
questions.explain: Pinned inputs make builds reproducible.

questions.q: A cache key is the date. What goes wrong?
options: It ignores the inputs: stale dependencies are restored after a lockfile change, or the cache misses daily; hash the lockfile instead
questions.explain: Hash inputs, not time.

questions.q: A 500-test suite where every test flakes 1% of the time is green how often on correct code?
questions.explain: Flakes compound, so a flake budget matters.

questions.q: The module has 100% coverage but a pricing bug passed CI. What was missing?
options: Assertions: coverage shows what ran, not that outputs were checked; consider mutation testing
questions.explain: Weak and strong suites can have identical coverage.

questions.q: A PR passes on its branch but main breaks after merging. What should the PR check run on?
options: The merged result (what will actually land on main), ideally via a merge queue
questions.explain: Two green branches can combine into a red build.

questions.q: Which setup limits damage if a PR from a fork is malicious?
options: No secrets for fork PRs, least-privilege token, and no pull_request_target checkout of untrusted code
questions.explain: Untrusted code must not meet privileged credentials.

questions.q: How should third-party actions be referenced?
options: Pinned to a full commit SHA (tags can be moved)
questions.explain: Rule W003 in the course linter.

questions.q: A deploy job lacks `concurrency:`. What can happen?
options: Two runs deploy at once and the older run may finish last, leaving the old version live
questions.explain: Serialise deploys per environment.

questions.q: Production approvals should live where?
options: On a protected environment with required reviewers and environment-scoped secrets
questions.explain: Protection rules gate secrets and jobs.

questions.q: You must rename a database column during a rolling deploy. What's the safe sequence?
options: Expand (add nullable new column), migrate data and code, then contract (drop the old column) in a later release
questions.explain: Old and new code overlap during rollouts.

questions.q: Which cannot be fixed by a rollback?
options: A destructive schema change, sent emails and payments
questions.explain: Rollbacks restore code, not data or side effects.

questions.q: Which deployment strategy gives instant switch-back but costs a whole second environment?
questions.explain: Keep the old environment alive until the new one is proven.

questions.q: A canary at 1% of 20,000 requests gets 200 canary requests. Why does the simulator wait for a minimum sample?
options: Small samples let a single error burst look like a real regression
questions.explain: min_canary protects against noise.

questions.q: Which two DORA measures describe stability?
options: Change failure rate and time to restore
questions.explain: The other two describe speed.

questions.q: A pipeline's wall-clock time is 18 minutes but billed minutes are 37. Why do they differ?
options: Wall-clock follows the critical path; billed time sums every job and matrix cell
questions.explain: Parallelism trades one for the other.

questions.q: A secret was pushed to a public repo and removed in the next commit. What now?
options: Revoke and rotate it immediately: Git history and forks keep it
questions.explain: Revoke first, investigate second.

questions.q: A migration from Jenkins to Actions is planned. What comes before converting pipelines?
options: Inventory: triggers, tools, credentials, runners and downstream consumers
questions.explain: You can't migrate what you haven't found.

challenges.title: Expand a build matrix
challenges.prompt: Implement expand_matrix(): the Cartesian product of the list-valued keys, remove combinations that match every key of an `exclude` entry, then apply each `include` (extend matching cells, or add a new job if it matches none). The sample matrix should yield 9 jobs.
challenges.starter:
import itertools

def expand_matrix(matrix):
    # Cartesian product of the list-valued keys, minus `exclude` matches,
    # then `include`: extend matching cells or add a new job if none match.
    return []

matrix = {
    "os": ["ubuntu", "windows", "macos"],
    "python": ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"],
    "exclude": [{"os": "macos", "python": "3.11"}],
    "include": [{"os": "ubuntu", "python": "3.14", "experimental": True}],

print(len(jobs))
for j in jobs:

challenges.title: Critical path and billed minutes

challenges.starter:

}

def critical_path(jobs):
    # longest chain of dependent jobs: return (total minutes, [job names in order])
    return 0, []

def billed(jobs):

length, path = critical_path(JOBS)
